title: Making plans
summary: A separable verb has a stressed prefix (opbellen). In a main clause and the imperative the prefix goes to the end: Ik bel je op. As an infinitive it stays whole: Ik wil je opbellen. be-, ver-, ont- never split.
explain:
A separable verb (*scheidbaar werkwoord*) is a verb with a small word in front, such as `op`, `mee`, `uit` or `af`. In the dictionary it is one word: `opbellen`, `meenemen`, `uitnodigen`. In a normal sentence the two parts often stand far apart. The prefix also changes the meaning: `gaan` is "to go", `uitgaan` is "to go out", `meegaan` is "to come along".

### The rule in a main clause

In a statement or a question the conjugated part stands where the verb always stands (second in a statement, first in a yes/no question), and the prefix goes to the **end** of the sentence. The conjugated part follows the normal rules of the present tense.

| | opbellen | meenemen |
| ik | bel … op | neem … mee |
| jij / je, u, hij, zij | belt … op | neemt … mee |
| wij, jullie, zij | bellen … op | nemen … mee |

> Ik bel je morgen op. — I will call you tomorrow.
> Mijn zus neemt een taart mee. — My sister is bringing a cake.
> Neem je iets te drinken mee? — Are you bringing something to drink?

Jij and je directly after the verb lose the t, as always: `Neem je … mee?`, `Ga je mee?`

Everything else comes between the two parts: the object, the time, `niet`. `Niet` stands just before the prefix.

> Het feest gaat zaterdag niet door. — The party is not going ahead on Saturday.

A phrase with a preposition may also come after the prefix, and in speech that is very common: `Ik nodig je uit voor mijn feest` and `Ik nodig je voor mijn feest uit` are both correct.

The simple past splits in the same way: `Ik belde je op` (unit A2 · 15).

### When it stays in one piece

When the verb is an **infinitive** at the end, it is written as one word. That happens after a modal verb, after `gaan` and after `zullen`.

> Ik wil je graag uitnodigen. — I would like to invite you.
> Kun je me morgen ophalen? — Can you pick me up tomorrow?

| form | example |
| present | Ik kom vanavond langs. |
| question | Kom je vanavond langs? |
| imperative | Kom vanavond langs! |
| with a modal | Ik kan vanavond langskomen. |
| perfect | Ik ben langsgekomen. |

The imperative splits too: `Bel me op!`, `Neem een jas mee!` In the perfect the `ge` goes in the middle: `opgebeld`, `meegenomen`, `uitgenodigd` (units A2 · 13 and A2 · 14). In a sub-clause the two parts come together again at the end; that is unit B1 · 17.

### Separable or not? Listen to the stress

A separable prefix is **stressed**: OPbellen, MEEnemen, UITnodigen, AFspreken. Most of these prefixes are also words of their own: `op, af, uit, mee, aan, in, weg, terug, thuis, langs`.

The prefixes **be-, ge-, her-, ont-, ver-, er-** are never stressed and **never split**: `betalen, gebruiken, herhalen, ontmoeten, vertellen, ervaren`. The stress is on the verb itself: beTAlen, verTELlen.

> Wie betaalt de drankjes? — Who is paying for the drinks?
> Ik ontmoet haar bij het station. — I am meeting her at the station.

A few prefixes, such as `door, over, onder, voor` and `om`, can be either, and then the stress decides. `VOORstellen` (to introduce, to propose) splits: `Ik stel je voor aan mijn vrienden`. But `overLEGgen` (to discuss) does not: `We overleggen morgen`.

### Watch out

- The prefix does not stay in front: *Ik opbel je → `Ik bel je op`.
- Do not forget the prefix: `Hij komt langs` (he drops by) is not `Hij komt` (he is coming). Without `mee`, `Ik neem een fles wijn` means "I take a bottle of wine", not "I bring one".
- After a modal verb nothing splits: *Ik wil je nodigen uit → `Ik wil je uitnodigen`.
- be-, ver-, ont- never split: *Ik taal de drankjes be → `Ik betaal de drankjes`.

### Compared with Ukrainian

Ukrainian also changes a verb's meaning with a prefix (`йти`, `прийти`, `піти`), but the prefix is always glued to the verb. In Dutch it travels to the end: `Я запрошую тебе` is `Ik nodig je uit`. So read a Dutch sentence to the end before you decide what the verb means.

words.en: to come along / to go along
to go ahead / to take place

sentences.nl: Ik nodig mijn buren uit voor mijn feest.
sentences.en: I am inviting my neighbours to my party.
sentences.note: nodig stands in second place and uit goes towards the end. The phrase voor mijn feest may come after uit or before it.
alt: Ik nodig mijn buren voor mijn feest uit.

sentences.nl: Neem jij een fles wijn mee?
sentences.en: Are you bringing a bottle of wine?
sentences.note: In a yes/no question neem comes first and mee goes to the very end. Jij follows the verb, so there is no t.
alt: Neem je een fles wijn mee?

sentences.note: After the question word comes spreken, and af closes the question. With zullen the verb would stay whole: Hoe laat zullen we afspreken?

sentences.en: My sister is dropping by tomorrow evening.
sentences.note: komt is the conjugated part (stem + t for mijn zus); langs goes to the end. Without langs it would only mean "is coming".

sentences.nl: Ga je vanavond mee naar de kroeg?
sentences.en: Are you coming along to the pub tonight?
sentences.note: Ga comes first and mee goes to the end, but the phrase naar de kroeg may follow mee, which is what people usually say.
alt: Ga jij vanavond mee naar de kroeg?
Ga je vanavond naar de kroeg mee?
Ga jij vanavond naar de kroeg mee?

sentences.nl: Ik wil je aan mijn vrienden voorstellen.
sentences.en: I want to introduce you to my friends.
sentences.note: After the modal verb wil, voorstellen is an infinitive at the end and stays in one piece.
alt: Ik wil jou aan mijn vrienden voorstellen.
Ik wil je voorstellen aan mijn vrienden.
Ik wil jou voorstellen aan mijn vrienden.

sentences.nl: Waarom zeg je de afspraak af?
sentences.en: Why are you cancelling the appointment?
sentences.note: zeg comes straight after the question word, without t because je follows it; af goes to the end, after the object.
alt: Waarom zeg jij de afspraak af?

sentences.nl: Het feest gaat zaterdag niet door.
sentences.en: The party is not going ahead on Saturday.
sentences.note: gaat is in second place and door at the end. Niet stands just before the prefix.
alt: Zaterdag gaat het feest niet door.

sentences.note: The imperative is the stem, and the separable verb splits here too: Neem … mee.

sentences.nl: Op een feest ontmoet je altijd nieuwe mensen.
sentences.en: At a party you always meet new people.
sentences.note: ontmoeten has the unstressed prefix ont-, so it never splits: ontmoet je, never "moet je … ont".
alt: Je ontmoet op een feest altijd nieuwe mensen.
Je ontmoet altijd nieuwe mensen op een feest.

exercises.nl: Ik ___ je na de bioscoop op.
exercises.en: I will call you after the cinema.
exercises.note: The prefix op is already at the end, so only the conjugated part goes in second place: bel. Ik takes the bare stem, without t.

exercises.en: I have to get up early tomorrow.
exercises.note: After the modal moet the separable verb is an infinitive at the end, written as one word: opstaan.

exercises.en: My friend goes out every Saturday.
exercises.note: uit is already at the end, so the gap needs only the conjugated part. Mijn vriendin is a hij/zij-subject: stem + t, gaat.

exercises.nl: Wat ___ (meenemen) jij mee naar het feest?
exercises.en: What are you bringing to the party?
exercises.note: Only neem goes in second place; mee is already in the sentence. Jij follows the verb, so there is no t.

exercises.en: My brother is dropping by this evening.
exercises.note: The conjugated part of langskomen is komen: mijn broer takes stem + t, komt. The prefix langs is at the end.

exercises.nl: Hoe laat ___ (opstaan) je na een feest op?
exercises.en: What time do you get up after a party?
exercises.note: sta is the conjugated part, and je directly after the verb means no t: sta je … op.

exercises.en: Why is he cancelling the concert?
exercises.note: The conjugated part zeggen becomes zegt for hij; af stays at the end of the question.
bel is the verb in second place, the pronoun je comes right after it, and op closes the sentence.

answers: Neem jij vanavond je gitaar mee?
Neem jij je gitaar vanavond mee?
exercises.en: Are you bringing your guitar tonight?
exercises.note: A yes/no question starts with the verb, then the subject. Mee goes to the very end; vanavond may stand before or after je gitaar.

answers: We willen jou voor onze borrel uitnodigen.
We willen jou uitnodigen voor onze borrel.
exercises.en: We want to invite you to our drinks.
exercises.note: After willen the infinitive uitnodigen stays in one piece at the end. The phrase voor onze borrel may also follow it.

answers: Morgen kom ik bij je langs.
Morgen kom ik langs bij je.
exercises.en: Tomorrow I will drop by at your place.
exercises.note: Morgen takes the first place, kom stays second and ik follows it. The prefix langs stays at the end.

exercises.task: Add the modal verb wil and use the infinitive uitgaan.
exercises.en: I want to go out tonight.
exercises.note: wil takes second place, and uitgaan goes to the end as one word.

exercises.task: Turn it into an instruction (the imperative) to one friend.
exercises.note: The imperative is the stem, neem, at the start. The separable verb splits as in any main clause: mee goes to the end.

exercises.en: I will call you back this evening.
exercises.note: In a main clause the prefix goes to the end: bel … terug. Terugbellen stays whole only as an infinitive.

exercises.wrong: Ik wil al mijn vrienden nodigen uit.
answers: Ik wil al mijn vrienden uitnodigen.
exercises.en: I want to invite all my friends.
exercises.note: After a modal verb the separable verb is an infinitive and stays in one piece: uitnodigen.

exercises.en: I am paying for the drinks.
exercises.note: be- is an unstressed prefix and never splits: betalen, ik betaal. The stress is on -taal.
